title: Unclog a bathroom sink by cleaning the P-trap
author: Lena K.
tools: slip-joint pliers (only if a nut is stuck)

steps.instruction: Clear everything out from under the sink and put an empty bucket directly under the U-shaped trap. Keep a towel next to it.
steps.expected_state: An empty bucket sits directly beneath the curved P-trap, with the trap and the bucket in the same frame and nothing else stored under the sink.
steps.verify_hints: Reject if no bucket is visible under the bend, or if the bucket is off to the side. A towel alone does not count. Bottles and cleaning products still in the cabinet are a fail.
common_mistakes: Loosening the nuts before the bucket is in place
Bucket too far to one side of the trap
steps.gate_requirement: Bucket positioned directly under the P-trap and the cabinet cleared, before any nut is touched.

steps.instruction: Loosen the two slip nuts on the trap by hand, turning them counterclockwise. If one will not budge, wrap it in the towel and use the pliers gently.
steps.expected_state: Both slip nuts are loosened and backed away from the trap joints, with the trap still hanging in place.
steps.verify_hints: Both nuts must visibly have moved away from the joints. If only one is loose, fail and say which one. A nut still tight against the joint is a fail.
common_mistakes: Using bare pliers on plastic and cracking the nut

steps.instruction: Pull the trap down and off, and tip it into the bucket. Pull out the hair and gunk with your fingers or the brush.
steps.expected_state: The P-trap is detached and held over or sitting in the bucket; the open ends of the tailpiece above and the trap arm from the wall are visible.
steps.verify_hints: The trap must be fully separated from both pipes. If it is still attached on one side, fail. Ask for a photo from below if the joint is hidden by a hand.
common_mistakes: Letting the washers fall into the bucket unnoticed
Tipping the trap out over the cabinet floor instead of the bucket

steps.instruction: Scrub the inside of the trap and the tailpiece with the brush. Then check both slip-joint washers for cracks and put them back with the tapered side facing the joint.
steps.expected_state: A clean trap interior with no hair or sludge, and two intact beveled washers sitting on the pipe ends.
steps.verify_hints: Look inside the trap: any visible clump of hair or sludge is a fail. Reject if a washer is missing or cracked. If the inside of the trap is not visible, ask for a photo looking straight into the opening.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the washer on the wall-side joint

steps.instruction: Slide the trap back onto the tailpiece and the trap arm, then hand-tighten both slip nuts clockwise. Snug, not forced.
steps.expected_state: The trap is reinstalled with both slip nuts threaded fully onto the joints, no gap at either joint, the trap hanging straight.
steps.verify_hints: Both nuts must be on the threads with no visible gap. If the trap sits crooked or a nut is cross-threaded at an angle, fail.
common_mistakes: Overtightening with pliers and cracking the nut

steps.instruction: Leave the bucket where it is and run the tap on full for a minute. Then press a dry paper towel or a dry finger under each slip nut and look for any wet mark.
steps.expected_state: The reinstalled trap with both slip nuts tight and both joints dry: no drip, no wet streak, no water on the towel or in the bucket, and the bucket still underneath.
steps.verify_hints: Any drop, bead or wet streak on a joint, or water collecting in the bucket, is a fail: say which nut to tighten a quarter turn. If the joints are not clearly visible, ask for a close photo of each nut. Running water does not need to be visible; dry joints after the test do.
common_mistakes: Removing the bucket before the test
